name: The Conservatory
description:
The Garfield Park Conservatory survived the flooding, the riots, the corporate annexation waves, and three separate arson attempts. It should not still be standing. The fact that it is — a cathedral of iron and glass rising from the wreckage of the West Side like a hallucination — says something about what people will fight to protect when everything else has been taken from them. The Conservatory is the largest enclosed green space in GLMZ's lower tiers, and it has become something its original architects never intended: a commons, a sanctuary, a black-market pharmacy, and the closest thing to neutral ground the West Side has.

Verdant Systems acquired the surrounding blocks in the 2040s, intending to convert the Conservatory into a corporate biolab. The neighborhood burned their survey drones out of the sky. Three times. Verdant pulled back to a perimeter and settled for a licensing arrangement — they supply the Conservatory's climate systems and gene-stock in exchange for first-refusal rights on any novel cultivars that emerge from the community gardens. It is, on paper, a partnership. In practice, it is a siege with better PR. The residents know that Verdant is waiting for the right crisis to justify a full acquisition, and they tend their plants with the focused intensity of people defending a border.

Inside the glass, the air is thick and wet and alive. The original botanical collections have been augmented with decades of guerrilla horticulture — medicinal plants, food crops, engineered oxygen-producers, and things nobody can identify that arrived as seeds in refugee pockets and found purchase in the Conservatory's soil. The Fern Room has become an unlicensed clinic where herbalists and rogue bioengineers treat lower-tier residents who cannot afford Lazarus Pharmaceuticals' pricing. The Palm House is a meeting ground where West Side faction leaders negotiate truces under canopies of engineered palms that clean the air faster than any corporate scrubber.

The surrounding blocks are standard West Side devastation — collapsed infrastructure, improvised housing, streets that flood every spring. But the Conservatory acts as an anchor, a proof that something can be maintained without corporate ownership. People come from across the Gray Zone to see it. Some of them cry. It is the only place in the lower tiers where you can smell earth instead of concrete, where the air tastes like it did before the city ate the sky.

sights: Iron-and-glass conservatory dome rising above crumbling West Side blocks like a landlocked lighthouse
Interior jungle of engineered plants, medicinal herbs, and unidentified cultivars climbing every surface
Verdant Systems perimeter drones circling the surrounding blocks at a respectful but watchful distance
Community gardens spreading outward from the Conservatory like green veins through gray concrete
Condensation streaming down interior glass panels, blurring the ruined cityscape outside into abstraction
Children playing between rows of food crops they helped plant
sounds: Water dripping through the Conservatory's misting systems — a sound like slow, patient rain
The hum of Verdant's climate-control units embedded in the walls
Birds — actual birds, not drones — nesting in the upper canopy
Quiet negotiation in the Palm House, voices kept low by mutual agreement
The crunch of gravel paths maintained by volunteer crews
smells: Living soil — the rarest smell in the lower tiers
Flowering medicinal plants from the Fern Room clinic
Wet iron from the Victorian-era frame sweating in the humidity
Compost heaps behind the west wing, rich and dark
atmosphere.feel: Hope as a physical structure. The Conservatory is the West Side's argument that beauty is not a luxury — it is infrastructure. Being inside it feels like stepping backward into a world that still believed in public things.

demographics: Predominantly Tier 1 and untier-ed residents from the surrounding West Side blocks. Climate refugees make up roughly 40% of the community, many of whom brought agricultural knowledge from the Gulf Coast Displacement Zone.
economy: The Conservatory's internal economy runs on barter and contribution — you tend the gardens, you eat from the gardens. Verdant Systems' licensing arrangement generates modest corporate credit that funds the climate systems. The Fern Room clinic operates on a sliding scale that slides all the way to zero.
power_structure: The Conservatory Council — an elected body of twelve gardeners — governs internal affairs. Verdant Systems controls the perimeter and the climate infrastructure, giving them leverage they have not yet fully exercised. Several West Side factions maintain informal truces within the glass walls.
dangers: Verdant Systems' acquisition pressure — one infrastructure failure away from a corporate takeover justification
Unlicensed bioengineered plants with unknown properties spreading through the collections
West Side faction conflicts that occasionally spill past the Conservatory's informal neutrality
Corporate espionage targeting novel cultivars developed by community herbalists
Structural degradation of the Victorian-era ironwork — the frame is 150 years old and counting
opportunities: The Fern Room clinic needs supplies and protection from Lazarus Pharmaceuticals' enforcement teams
Verdant Systems pays well for information about what is actually growing inside the Conservatory
The Conservatory Council hires freelancers to run interference against corporate survey operations
Novel medicinal cultivars fetch premium prices on the Circuit's gray market
Neutral ground for negotiations that cannot happen anywhere else on the West Side
story_hooks: A plant nobody recognizes is growing in the deep collection — it appeared overnight, it is spreading, and Verdant Systems is suddenly very interested in renegotiating their licensing agreement

The Conservatory Council has received an anonymous offer to fund full independence from Verdant — but the source traces back to Carrion Defense Works, and nobody can figure out why a weapons manufacturer wants to protect a garden
Someone is poisoning the soil in the community gardens outside the glass walls, methodically, block by block
frequented_by: West Side residents maintaining community garden plots
Herbalists and rogue bioengineers operating the Fern Room clinic
Verdant Systems monitors and corporate liaisons
Faction negotiators using the Palm House as neutral ground
Refugees from the Gulf Coast Displacement Zone with agricultural expertise
